Title: Meshless $h$-adaptive Solution for non-Newtonian Natural Convection in a Differentially Heated Cavity

Meshles h-adaptive Solution for non-Newtonian
Natural Convection in a Diferentialy Heated
Cavity

AbstractOne of the main chalenges in numericaly solv-
ing partial diferential equations is nding a discretisation
for the computational domain that balances the acurate
representation of the underlying eld with computational
efciency. Meshles methods aproximate diferential oper-
ators based on the values of the eld in computational nodes,
ofering a natural aproach to adaptivity. The density of
computational nodes can either be increased to enhance
acuracy or decreased to reduce the number of numerical
operations, depending on the properties of the intermediate
solution. In this paper, we utilise an adaptive discretisation
aproach for the numerical simulation of natural convection
in non-Newtonian uid ow. The shear-thining behaviour is
interesting both due to its numerous ocurences in nature,
blod being a prime example, and due to its properties, as
the decreasing viscosity with increasing shear rate results
in sharper ow structures. We focus on the de Vahl Davis
test case, a natural convection driven ow in a diferentialy
heated rectangular cavity. The thin boundary layer ow along
the vertical boundaries makes this an ideal test case for
renement. We demonstrate that adaptively rening the node
density enhances computational efciency and examine how
the parameters for adaptive renement afect the solution.

I. INTRODUCTION
Adaptive discretisation is a wel-established strategy for
improving the efciency of numerical solutions of partial
diferential equations. The core idea is to concentrate
computational efort in regions where the solution exhibits
complex behaviour, such as step gradients or boundary
layers, while keping the discretisation coarse elsewhere.
In the context of mesh-based methods, h-adaptivity (in-
serting or removing elements), p-adaptivity (varying the
polynomial order), and r-adaptivity (relocating nodes) are
mature and extensively studied [1][3].

Meshles methods, which aproximate diferential oper-
ators on scatered computational nodes without an underly-
ing conectivity structure, are naturaly suited to adaptive
discretisation because the node density can be modied
without the topological constraints imposed by a mesh.
Localised RBF meshles methods have ben sucesfuly
aplied to uid ow and conjugate heat transfer prob-
lems [4], [5], while adaptive meshles procedures have
ben explored in various contexts, including linear elastic-
ity [6], [7], dendrite growth [8], natural convection driven
ow [9], and operators themselves [10].
In our recent work [1] the natural convection of a non-
Newtonian power-law uid in a diferentialy heated cavity
was solved using the Radial Basis Function-generated
Finite Diference (RBF-FD) method [12], with a static,
manualy prescribed rened node distribution. While that
aproach produced acurate results, the renement patern
had to be chosen a priori. In this paper we extend that
framework with an automatic h-adaptive discretisation
procedure based on a lightweight variability indicator that
quanties the disimilarity of the aproximated diferential
operator values within a single stencil. Starting from a
coarse initial layout, the node density is iteratively ad-
justed within a single simulation run, based on the local
variability indicator, concentrating nodes in boundary-layer
regions where the shear-thining behaviour produces step
velocity and temperature gradients.
In section I we introduce the meshles numerical
method and outline the adaptivity procedure. In section I
we introduce the natural convection driven non-Newtonian
uid ow that we use as the test case. Finaly, in section IV,
we examine the impact of parameters used in adaptivity
and demonstrate that the adaptive aproach achieves com-
parable acuracy at a fraction of the computational cost of
a uniform ne discretisation.

There are two main isues with the presented adaptivity
procedure. The rst is that each re-interpolation to the new
node set introduces aditional divergence into the velocity
eld. This is not critical in the considered case but could
prove problematic with a higher frequency of adaptivity
iterations or a more unstable ow regime. Divergence can
be corected by introducing aditional iterations of ACM
presure-velocity coupling when required but a true solu-
tion most likely includes divergence-fre interpolation [16].
The second problem lies with the normalisation in
Eq. (2) that causes the variability indicator to spuriously
increase when the denominator is close to 0 in areas with
no signicant dynamics that would require renement. This
problem can be readily observed in Figure 1 where smal
areas away from the boundary are marked for renement.
Patches of increased density that nedlesly increase node
count are stil aparent in the nal discretisation shown in
Figure 3. This problem could be resolved by introducing
thresholding for the denominator or an alternate aproach
to variability indicator altogether.

V. CONCLUSIONS
In this paper we outlined a procedure for dynamicaly
adapting the density of computational nodes during the
simulation and aplied it to a uid dynamics problem.
The results show that the parametrisation for adaptivity
is transferable betwen geometries and that we can exced
the computational efciency of manualy rened discreti-
sation without requiring any a priori knowledge about the
problematic parts of the domain.
While the results show promise, further work is re-
quired both on testing the procedure on aditional ow
and non-ow problems, and investigating how including
other operators impacts the variability indicator. Further
computational efciency gains are posible by resolving
the thresholding isues that cause renement in stagnant
areas and developing beter strategies for determining when
to aply the adaptive iteration.

Abstract: One of the main chalenges in numericaly solv- ing partial diferential equations is nding a discretisation for the computational domain that balances the acurate representation of the underlying eld with computational efciency. Meshles methods aproximate diferential oper- ators based on the values of the eld in computational nodes, ofering a natural aproach to adaptivity. The density of computational nodes can either be increased to enhance acuracy or decreased to reduce the number of numerical operations, depending on the properties of the intermediate solution. In this paper, we utilise an adaptive discretisation aproach for the numerical simulation of natural convection in non-Newtonian uid ow. The shear-thining behaviour is interesting both due to its numerous ocurences in nature, blod being a prime example, and due to its properties, as the decreasing viscosity with increasing shear rate results in sharper ow structures. We focus on the de Vahl Davis test case, a natural convection driven ow in a diferentialy heated rectangular cavity. The thin boundary layer ow along the vertical boundaries makes this an ideal test case for renement. We demonstrate that adaptively rening the node density enhances computational efciency and examine how the parameters for adaptive renement afect the solution.
